data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future truth, but as a non-inductive, methodological rule of 'critical rationality' that maximizes the potential for error detection; accepting this costs us the comfort of believing our actions are probabilistically safe, forcing us to acknowledge that acting on the best-tested theory is a responsible gamble where failure remains logically possible and indeed desired for progress.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If corroboration is shown to implicitly rely on the uniformity of nature assumption.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's distinction between acting and believing collapses under pragmatic pressure (e.g., building a bridge requires belief in safety, not just error detection).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'gamble' analogy fails to explain why scientists feel justified in expecting success rather than just hoping for informative failure.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification of belief' (which Popper rejects) and 'justification of action' (which he accepts via critical preference). It posits that choosing the most severely tested theory is rational because it has withstood the strongest attempts at falsification, thereby offering the most informative basis for action. If it fails, we learn more than if a weakly tested theory fails. This preference does not assume the future will resemble the past (induction) but rather adopts a rule: 'Act on the hypothesis that has survived the most stringent criticism so far,' which is a deductive consequence of the goal to eliminate error, not a prediction of success.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
